Background: Surgical therapy is required in the majority of peri-implantitis cases due to the inconsistent efficacy of non-surgical approaches. Although surgical treatment generally offers higher predictability, reported success rates vary widely.
Aim: To review the available evidence on the factors influencing the outcomes of peri- implantitis surgical therapy, including surgical technique, implant-site characteristics, and patient-related conditions.
Materials and Methods: This narrative review is based on a literature search conducted in three electronic databases to identify relevant studies published between January 2010 and November 2025.

1 | INTRODUCTION Owing to the inconsistent efficacy of non-surgical approaches for peri-implantitis management, surgical intervention is required in the majority of cases. 1 Following implant surface decontamination, several surgical strategies can be employed, including non- reconstructive therapy, resective procedures involving hard-and/ or soft-tissue removal, and reconstructive techniques utilizing bone grafting procedures. 2,3 The choice of surgical approach is largely determined by the morphology of the peri-implant bone defect. 4 Accordingly, more favorable outcomes of reconstructive therapy have been reported in the presence of a contained defect configuration (i.e., supported by 3-to 4-walls) compared with non-contained defects.

Therefore, the aim of this narrative review is to provide an overview of the factors influencing the effectiveness of surgical therapy for peri-implantitis.

2 | LITERATURE SEARCH STRATEGY A comprehensive literature search was conducted for this narrative review using electronic databases (PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library) to identify relevant studies published between January 2010 and November 2025. Conclusions: Outcomes of surgical peri-implantitis treatment are determined by a complex interplay of defect morphology, disease severity, implant surface characteristics, surgical expertise, and patient adherence to supportive care.
Clinical Relevance: Clinically, careful case selection, defect-specific surgical planning, and strict postoperative maintenance are essential to enhance predictability and long- term stability.

3 | SURGICAL FACTORS 3.1 | Flap design Flap design during surgical peri-implantitis treatment should provide adequate access to the defect while minimizing surgical trauma and postoperative discomfort for patients. Table S1 summarizes the incision techniques and flap designs used in the included studies.

For the non-reconstructive/resective treatment modalities, the majority of studies employed a conventional full-thickness access flap, typically a mid-crestal incision often combined with relieving vertical incisions to ensure adequate visibility and instrumentation of the defect. In most cases of non-reconstructive surgery, the flaps were repositioned apically or sutured to allow pocket elimination and secondary intention healing of soft tissues.
For reconstructive therapies, most studies likewise utilized full- thickness flaps with broad access, aiming for primary wound closure over the augmented defect.

Flaps were generally repositioned to cover the regenerative materials and sutured for tension-free primary closure (often requiring periosteal releasing incisions). It should be pointed out that compared with periodontitis, peri-implantitis lesions are often significantly larger and frequently require circumferential access to adequately debride and decontaminate the implant surface. 17 Thus, in practice, a greater flap elevation is typically needed around peri- implantitis sites than around periodontitis sites.
Interestingly, a novel flapless surgical approach has been explored recently as an alternative to traditional flap elevation. In a large prospective case series including 117 patients (338 implants), a flapless surgical access (pocket curettage without raising a flap) led to disease resolution at 54.4% of implants over a follow-up period of 5 years.

3.4 | Significance of a barrier membrane The principle of GBR involves placing a barrier membrane over the graft material thereby creating a space for bone regeneration. 36 A membrane can also help stabilize the graft and maintain the augmented contour. Generally, using a membrane should improve regenerative outcomes in peri-implantitis defects, particularly in non-contained defects where graft stability is a challenge.
Summary of the findings: The clinical significance of adding a barrier membrane in peri-implantitis reconstructive therapy remains controversial.

of the findings: The clinical significance of adding a barrier membrane in peri-implantitis reconstructive therapy remains controversial. One 4-year study reported significantly greater BOP and PD reductions when a xenogenic bone graft was combined with a native collagen membrane, compared with sites treated with a graft alone. It is plausible that in partially contained defects (1-or 2-wall scenarios), the membrane plays a more critical role in preventing soft-tissue collapse and maintaining the graft, whereas in inherently contained 4-wall defects, a membrane might confer little added benefit. In summary, current data do not show a clear overall clinical benefit to using barrier membranes in reconstructive peri-implantitis therapy, especially given the potential for increased patient morbidity.

3.5 | Defect configuration 3.5.1 | Reconstructive therapy Peri-implantitis lesions can present various bone defect morphologies.
Commonly, defects are classified as Class I (intrabony defects with a surrounding bony wall), Class II (supracrestal horizontal bone loss), or Class III (combined intrabony and supracrestal defects). 41 Clinical data indicate that the majority of peri-implantitis sites (around 79%) are combination defects (Class III). 41 Pure intrabony lesions often show circumferential bone loss with intact buccal and lingual walls (true 4-wall circumferential defects, observed in about 55% of intrabony cases), followed by 3-wall defects (e.g., facial dehiscence- type defects). 41 Pure horizontal defects (Class II) are relatively uncommon (as low as about 2% of lesions) ( Figure 2).

3.6 | Flap adaptation and postoperative healing mode A critical intra-and postoperative consideration is whether the surgical site is left to heal in a submerged (completely covered) or a non-submerged (transmucosal) mode. Basically, flap adaptation techniques, suturing methods, and the decision to submerge the implant during healing can influence outcomes by affecting wound stability and infection control.

suturing methods, and the decision to submerge the implant during healing can influence outcomes by affecting wound stability and infection control.
In periodontal surgery, apically repositioned flaps are often used in resective treatment to reduce pockets, whereas primary closure is sought in regenerative procedures. Similar principles may also be applied at peri-implantitis sites:
• For non-reconstructive surgical therapy, clinicians may consider repositioning the flaps apically or at least ensuring they are not completely covering the implant to maximize post-surgical pocket depth reduction. This approach may facilitate an open drainage if needed and reduces the risk of deep residual pockets.
• For reconstructive therapy, achieving primary closure and, if possible, submerged healing is thought to promote more predictable bone regeneration.

For reconstructive therapy, achieving primary closure and, if possible, submerged healing is thought to promote more predictable bone regeneration. Submerged healing isolates the defect site from the oral environment during early healing, potentially leading to superior outcomes.
Evidence from a preclinical canine study supports submerged healing. In particular, surgically treated peri-implantitis defects that were kept submerged for 3 months had significantly higher bone-to- implant contact than those that healed with transmucosal healing. 47 Clinically, a reanalysis of two prospective studies compared outcomes of reconstructive therapy under submerged vs. non-submerged conditions.

Indeed, early postoperative wound dehiscence has been frequently reported with submerged healing in reconstructive peri-implantitis therapy, with one study noting dehiscences in 25 of 36 sites despite primary closure attempts. 50 Since such complications can compromise treatment outcomes, clinicians should carefully consider flap management in reconstructive therapy.

3.7 | Systemic antibiotics Considering the bacterial etiology of peri-implantitis, systemic antibiotics have been investigated as adjunctive therapy in combination with surgical management. The rationale is that reducing the bacterial load systemically could enhance the effect of mechanical debridement and implant surface decontamination during surgery. Here we summarize the findings from studies of systemic antibiotic use in peri-implantitis surgery, including non- reconstructive and reconstructive approaches.

6 | CONCLUDING REMARKS Surgical peri-implantitis treatment outcomes are influenced by a multitude of factors spanning surgical technique, local site characteristics, and patient-level behaviors.

treatment outcomes are influenced by a multitude of factors spanning surgical technique, local site characteristics, and patient-level behaviors. Key conclusions from the current evidence include:
Surgical factors • The adjunctive use of reconstructive (regenerative) measures generally improves radiographic defect fill and may help maintain soft-tissue levels, but no clear advantage has been shown in resolving clinical signs of inflammation compared with non- reconstructive open-flap debridement.
• Reconstructive protocols that incorporate slowly resorbing bone substitutes (e.g., xenografts) tend to yield more favorable outcomes than those using autogenous bone, particularly in terms of bone fill and possibly pocket reduction.
• There is insufficient evidence to support the routine use of biologics (growth factors, EMD, PRF, etc.)

• Contained intrabony defects (3-and 4-wall) show considerably more favorable outcomes with reconstructive therapy compared with non-contained 1-or 2-wall defects.
• No clear clinical benefits could be observed for the adjunctive use of a membrane in reconstructive therapy. Their application should be weighed against defect morphology (more justified in 1–3 wall defects and possibly unnecessary in 4-wall defects).
• The effectiveness of peri-implantitis surgery is tied to the surgeon's experience and technique, with experienced surgeons achieving higher success rates.
